card.name: Kartik Naach
card.tagline: A centuries-old Newar musical theatre tradition performed annually in Patan, Nepal.
card.profile: Kartik Naach is a traditional Newar musical theatre performed annually in Patan Durbar Square, Nepal, during the month of Kartik. Established in 1641 by King Siddhi Narsingh Malla, the performance depicts 17 tales of the Hindu god Vishnu. The tradition is managed by the Kartik Nach Preservation Committee and involves dancers portraying deities such as Barahi, Ganesh, Shiva, and Krishna. Despite the 2015 earthquake, the community continues to perform the dance in the open-air setting of Kartik Dabali.
card.insight: King Siddhi Narsingh Malla established this dance-drama in 1641, and it has expanded from a two-day performance to a 27-day cycle depicting 17 tales of the Hindu god Vishnu.
card.profile_long:
Kartik Naach, known in the Newar language as कात्तिक प्याखं, represents a significant historical and cultural pillar of the Newar community in Nepal. The tradition was inaugurated in 1641 AD by King Siddhi Narsingh Malla. Initially, the performance was a modest two-day affair. Over the subsequent generations, the scope of the drama expanded significantly through the contributions of the royal lineage. King Siddhi Narsingh Malla's son, Srinivas Malla, extended the duration by seven days, and his grandson, Yog Narendra Malla, added another 15 days, bringing the total cycle to its current potential of 27 days. This extended duration allows for the enactment of 17 distinct tales centered on the Hindu god Vishnu.

The performance takes place at the Kartik Dabali in Patan Durbar Square. A unique architectural feature associated with the dance is the golden window in Patan, which is opened specifically for the duration of the play. Legends suggest that this window was constructed to honor King Siddhi Narsingh Malla. The performance is deeply rooted in religious observance, featuring dancers who portray various Hindu deities, including Barahi, Ganesh, Shiva, and Krishna. These dancers are adorned in colorful costumes and wear festoons around their necks, creating a visual representation of the divine characters they embody. The music and dance compositions are largely attributed to King Siddhi Narsingh Malla, though minor changes have occurred over the centuries.

The preservation of Kartik Naach has evolved from royal patronage to community-led stewardship. While the Kartik Naach Prabandhan Samiti historically maintained the tradition, the Kartik Nach Preservation Committee (KNPC) has taken over this responsibility since 2013. The scale of the production is substantial; in 2015, the performance involved 45 musicians and 10 helpers. The resilience of this tradition was tested during the April 2015 Nepal earthquake, which caused critical damage to the Patan Durbar Square. Despite the destruction, the performance continued just seven months later, with the dance-drama being held for 10 nights amidst the ruins. This event highlighted the deep connection between the local population and the performance, as thousands of people, both young and old, gathered to watch the open-air presentation. The significance of the dance is also reflected in local governance support, such as the 2018 allocation of 200,000 Nepalese rupees by the Lalitpur authorities to support the production. Hari Man Shrestha, a former director of the KNPC, has documented the history and details of the play in a dedicated book, ensuring that the knowledge of this complex musical theatre is preserved for future generations.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance was started in 1641 AD by King Siddhi Narsingh Malla. It began as a two-day performance, later expanded by his son Srinivas Malla and grandson Yog Narendra Malla to cover 17 tales of Vishnu over 27 days.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers portray Hindu deities including Barahi, Ganesh, Shiva, and Krishna. They wear colorful clothes and festoons around their necks. The performance is held in an open-air setting.
sections.music_and_instruments: The performance is accompanied by folk music. In 2015, the production utilized 45 musicians to support the dance-drama.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance is performed at the Kartik Dabali in Patan Durbar Square. Dancers wear colorful costumes and festoons. A golden window, opened only for the play, is a key feature of the setting.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed annually in the month of Kartik (October or November) to honor the Hindu god Vishnu through 17 tales.
sections.notable_figures: King Siddhi Narsingh Malla (founder), Srinivas Malla (son), Yog Narendra Malla (grandson), and Hari Man Shrestha (former director of KNPC and author).
